title: WhatsApp Replaces Six-Digit PINs With Full Passwords, Adds Multiple Passkeys
excerpt: Meta's messaging platform overhauls two-step verification, expands passkey support beyond one billion users, and gives Android callers new scam warnings.
body:
• WhatsApp is replacing six-digit PINs with full alphanumeric passwords for two-step verification, dramatically expanding the credential space against brute-force attacks
  • Users can now register multiple passkeys across iOS and Android devices, with more than one billion people already using passkey login
  • Android users will see new caller context for unknown numbers, including the caller's country of origin and shared group memberships

WhatsApp on Tuesday announced a trio of security upgrades targeting account takeovers and scam calls, its most significant authentication overhaul since introducing two-step verification years ago.

The changes address a persistent vulnerability: while WhatsApp's end-to-end encryption protects message content, attackers have repeatedly exploited the authentication and recovery process to hijack accounts. The platform's 2.7 billion users have long relied on a six-digit PIN as their second verification factor — a credential with just one million possible combinations.

Passwords Replace PINs

The most consequential change upgrades two-step verification from a numeric PIN to a full password supporting letters, numbers, and special characters. The shift vastly increases the credential space, making brute-force attacks computationally impractical even without rate-limiting protections.

"WhatsApp is now replacing that PIN with a proper password. That means you'll be able to create something longer and more difficult to guess, using letters and numbers as well as special characters."

— Digital Trends

Users who already enabled two-step verification can upgrade their existing PIN to a password through settings. New users activating the feature will set a password from the start.

Multi-Device Passkey Support

WhatsApp is also expanding passkey functionality to allow multiple passkeys per account. The platform reported that more than one billion users now log in with a passkey — a milestone that underscores the technology's rapid adoption since its Android launch in 2023 and iOS expansion in 2024.

Passkeys use public-key cryptography stored on the device, letting users authenticate with Face ID, Touch ID, or a screen lock instead of typing codes. An attacker would need physical access to the registered device, effectively neutralizing remote phishing attempts. Multi-device support means users who operate WhatsApp on both an iPhone and an Android tablet can register separate passkeys for each.

Caller Context for Unknown Numbers

The third update, currently limited to Android, displays additional information when an unsaved number calls. Users will now see whether the caller's number originates from another country and whether they share any WhatsApp groups.

"Scammers rely on urgency — now you can take a beat with some more info before answering."

— WhatsApp

The feature targets social engineering attacks where scammers impersonate banks, delivery services, or acquaintances calling from abroad. By surfacing geographic and social context before a user picks up, WhatsApp aims to disrupt the urgency scammers depend on.

Part of a Broader Security Push

The updates follow a series of security additions throughout 2025 and 2026. Earlier this year, WhatsApp introduced Strict Account Settings for high-risk users such as journalists and activists, blocking media from unknown senders and locking several privacy toggles. In mid-August, the platform rolled out Scam Alert, an optional AI-powered feature that flags suspicious messages from non-contacts without sending content to Meta's servers.

Despite these layers, challenges persist. Account compromise stories continue to circulate, often involving social engineering that tricks users into sharing verification codes or exploiting weaknesses in linked devices and web sessions. The new password requirement will not help users who have already lost access, and recovery still demands the original phone number in most cases.

For the Indian diaspora, where WhatsApp serves as the dominant channel for family communication, group coordination, and even small business transactions, each security upgrade carries outsized importance. Account takeovers do not just compromise personal privacy — they can disrupt the cross-border lifelines that connect millions of families across time zones.
